title: Deploying AI Apps (MLOps)
blurb: Ship it: call model APIs, wrap them in your own service, serve open models, and watch cost, speed and quality.

lessons.title: Your first LLM API call
lessons.summary: API keys, the SDK and the Messages API.
body: Chat apps are one way to use an LLM. An **API** is the other: your own program sends text to the model over the internet and gets a reply back. This is how you build the model into your own app.

First you create an **API key** in the provider's console. It is like a password that also pays the bill, so keep it secret: store it in an environment variable such as `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, never paste it into code you share or into a web page.

Next you install the provider's **SDK** (a helper library, here `pip install anthropic`). With the **Messages API** you send a `model` name, a `max_tokens` limit for the reply, an optional `system` prompt, and a list of `messages`, each with a `role` (`user` or `assistant`) and `content`.

The response holds the reply as a list of content blocks, plus useful extras: the `stop_reason` (did it finish, or hit the token limit?) and `usage`, the number of input and output tokens you are billed for. The API does not remember past calls, so for a conversation you send the earlier messages again each time.
The code makes one real call. It needs an API key and internet access, so run it on your computer or in Google Colab.
keyIdeas: An API lets your own code send prompts and receive replies.
Keep your API key secret, in an environment variable.
A request has a model, max_tokens, optional system prompt and messages.
The API is stateless: resend earlier messages to continue a chat.

quiz.q: Where should you keep your API key?
options: In the JavaScript of your public website
In an environment variable on your machine or server
In the prompt so the model knows it
quiz.explain: Environment variables keep secrets out of code and out of anything users can see.

quiz.q: How does the model remember earlier turns of a conversation when using the API?
options: You send the previous messages again with each request
quiz.explain: The Messages API is stateless, so the conversation history travels in each request.

code.title: first_call.py
code.source:
# pip install anthropic
# Set your key first:  export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()   # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

message = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system="You are a friendly tutor. Answer in two sentences.",
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "What is a neural network?"},
    ],
)

# The reply is a list of content blocks; print the text ones
for block in message.content:
    if block.type == "text":
        print(block.text)

print("Stop reason:", message.stop_reason)
print("Tokens in/out:", message.usage.input_tokens, message.usage.output_tokens)
code.note: Needs an API key and internet, so run it in Google Colab or on your computer.

lessons.title: Wrap it in your own API
lessons.summary: A minimal FastAPI service with automatic docs.
body: You should not call the LLM directly from a web page, because the browser would need your secret API key. Instead you put a small **backend service** in the middle: the page calls your service, and your service calls the model.

**FastAPI** is a popular Python framework for this. You write ordinary functions and decorate them with a route, like `@app.post("/summarize")`. Think of it as a restaurant: the menu (routes) says what you can order, and the kitchen (your function) does the work out of sight.

You describe the shape of requests and responses with **Pydantic** models. FastAPI then checks incoming data for you (wrong types get a clear error) and automatically builds interactive documentation at `/docs`, where you can try every endpoint in the browser.

Your service is also where production concerns live: keeping the key secret, limiting text length, adding a `/health` route so hosting platforms can check it is alive, logging requests, and later adding caching or rate limits.
The code is a complete small service with a health check and a summarize endpoint. It needs to run on a real machine, so try it on your computer.
keyIdeas: Never call the LLM from the browser; put a backend in between.
FastAPI turns Python functions into web endpoints.
Pydantic models validate requests and power automatic docs at /docs.
Your service is the place for secrets, limits, logging and health checks.

quiz.q: Why put a backend between your web page and the LLM API?
options: To keep the API key secret and control usage
quiz.explain: The server holds the key and can validate, limit and log requests.

quiz.q: What does FastAPI generate automatically at /docs?
quiz.explain: FastAPI reads your routes and Pydantic models to build interactive docs.

code.title: main.py
code.note: Needs FastAPI, an API key and a server, so run it on your computer with `fastapi dev main.py`.

lessons.title: Serving open models
lessons.summary: Run locally with Ollama or serve with vLLM.
body: Instead of paying per call to a hosted model, you can run an **open-weights** model yourself. Your data never leaves your machine, there is no per-token bill, and you can work offline. The trade-off is that you supply the hardware, and small local models are less capable than the largest hosted ones.

**Ollama** is the easiest way to start on a laptop. One command like `ollama run llama3.2` downloads a model and lets you chat with it. In the background it runs a local server on port 11434 that your code can call, much like a cloud API.

**vLLM** is built for serving many users on GPUs. It uses tricks such as **PagedAttention** (managing memory like pages in a book) and **continuous batching** (adding new requests to a running batch) to handle much more traffic. It exposes an **OpenAI-compatible API**, so existing client code can point at it by changing the URL.

A simple rule: Ollama for trying models and personal projects on your own computer, vLLM when you deploy a model on a GPU server for real traffic. Either way, pick a model size that fits your memory; quantized (compressed) versions make bigger models fit.
The code calls a local Ollama server. It needs Ollama running on your computer, so it cannot run in the browser.
keyIdeas: Self-hosting open models keeps data local and avoids per-token fees.
Ollama: one command to download and run a model on a laptop.
vLLM: high-throughput GPU serving with an OpenAI-compatible API.
Choose a model size, or quantized version, that fits your hardware.

quiz.q: Which tool is designed for high-throughput serving on GPU servers?
quiz.explain: vLLM uses PagedAttention and continuous batching to serve many requests efficiently.

quiz.q: What is a main benefit of running a model locally?
options: It is always smarter than hosted models
Your data stays on your own machine
quiz.explain: Local models process data on your hardware, which helps with privacy.

code.title: ollama_call.py
code.source:
# First, in a terminal:  ollama pull llama3.2   (Ollama serves on port 11434)
import requests

response = requests.post(
    "http://localhost:11434/api/chat",
    json={
        "model": "llama3.2",
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain a GPU in one sentence."}],
        "stream": False,          # get one complete JSON reply
    },
)
print(response.json()["message"]["content"])

# vLLM serves an OpenAI-compatible API instead:
#   vllm serve Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct
# then POST to http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions
code.note: Needs Ollama installed and running, so run it on your own computer.

lessons.title: Architecture of a GenAI app
lessons.summary: RAG, guardrails, routing, caching and observability together.

resources.title: Chip Huyen: Building A Generative AI Platform

body: A real GenAI product is more than one model call. It is a pipeline of small parts, a bit like an airport: security check, ticket desk, routing to the right gate, the flight itself, and a control tower watching everything.

Requests usually pass through: **input guardrails** (block abuse or injection attempts), a **cache** (return a saved answer for repeat questions), **retrieval** (RAG fetches relevant documents), a **router** (send easy questions to a cheap, fast model and hard ones to a strong model), the **model call**, and **output guardrails** (check for leaks or unsafe content).
Around it all sits **observability**: logs of every request, which model handled it, how long it took and what it cost. Without this you cannot debug problems or know where the money goes.

Do not build every piece on day one. Start with a single model call, then add each part when you have a reason: retrieval when answers lack knowledge, a cache when costs grow, guardrails as soon as real users arrive.
The code is a toy version of the whole pipeline in about 40 lines, with a fake model, so you can see each stage do its job, including a cache hit and a blocked attack.
keyIdeas: A GenAI app is a pipeline, not a single model call.
Guardrails check both what goes in and what comes out.
Caching and routing cut cost; retrieval adds knowledge.
Start simple and add components only when you need them.

quiz.q: What does a router do in a GenAI app?
options: Sends each request to a suitable model, e.g. cheap for easy questions
quiz.explain: Routing matches request difficulty to model cost and capability.

quiz.q: Which component returns a saved answer for a repeated question?
quiz.explain: A cache stores earlier responses so repeat requests skip the model call.

lessons.title: Cost and latency
lessons.summary: Fewer tokens, streaming, parallel calls and prompt caching.
body: LLM APIs charge per **token**, and output tokens usually cost several times more than input tokens. Latency, the wait for an answer, grows with the number of tokens generated. So the first rule for both cost and speed is the same: **use fewer tokens**, especially fewer output tokens.

Trim long prompts, ask for short answers, and use a smaller model for easy jobs. **Prompt caching** helps when many requests share the same long beginning, such as a big system prompt or document: the provider stores that prefix and charges much less to reuse it, and the response starts faster.

**Streaming** sends the reply word by word as it is generated. The total time is about the same, but users see text almost immediately, which feels far faster, like a video that starts playing before it has fully downloaded.

If you need several independent model calls, run them **in parallel** instead of one after another. Then you wait only as long as the slowest call, not the sum of all of them. For work that is not urgent, batch APIs process requests later at a discount.
The code does the math for a busy app: daily cost with and without caching, sequential versus parallel calls, and what streaming changes. The prices are example numbers, not real quotes.
keyIdeas: Fewer tokens means lower cost and lower latency.
Prompt caching makes a repeated long prefix cheaper and faster.
Streaming shows the first words early, so the app feels fast.
Run independent calls in parallel: wait for the slowest, not the sum.

quiz.q: Three independent calls take 1, 2 and 3 seconds. Roughly how long if run in parallel?
quiz.explain: In parallel you only wait for the slowest call.

options: How quickly the user sees the first words
The size of the context window
quiz.explain: Streaming shows text as it is generated, cutting the perceived wait.

code.title: cost_math.py
code.source:
# Back-of-the-envelope cost and latency math (example prices, not real quotes)
PRICE_IN, PRICE_OUT = 3.00, 15.00          # dollars per million tokens
CACHE_READ = 0.10 * PRICE_IN               # cached input is far cheaper

def cost(tokens_in, tokens_out, cached=0):
    fresh = tokens_in - cached
    return (fresh * PRICE_IN + cached * CACHE_READ + tokens_out * PRICE_OUT) / 1e6

requests_per_day = 10_000
system_prompt, question, answer = 4_000, 200, 300   # tokens

base = cost(system_prompt + question, answer)
cached = cost(system_prompt + question, answer, cached=system_prompt)
shorter = cost(system_prompt + question, 120, cached=system_prompt)

print(f"Per day, no caching       : ${base * requests_per_day:8.2f}")
print(f"Per day, cache the prompt : ${cached * requests_per_day:8.2f}")
print(f"... and shorter answers   : ${shorter * requests_per_day:8.2f}")

# Latency: three independent calls, each ~1.2 s
calls = [1.2, 1.1, 1.3]
print(f"\nSequential calls take ~{sum(calls):.1f} s")
print(f"Parallel calls take   ~{max(calls):.1f} s (wait only for the slowest)")

# Streaming doesn't make the total faster, but the first words appear early
time_to_first_token, tokens_per_sec = 0.4, 80
print(f"Streaming: first words after {time_to_first_token} s, "
      f"full answer after {time_to_first_token + answer / tokens_per_sec:.1f} s")

lessons.title: Monitoring and observability
lessons.summary: Trace model calls and watch for drift.
body: Once your app is live, you need to see what it is doing. **Observability** means recording enough about each request to answer "what happened and why?" later, like a flight recorder on a plane.

The core tool is a **trace**: a record of one request, including the prompt, the retrieved documents, each model call, the response, the latency, token counts and cost. Tools like Langfuse collect traces and let you search them when a user reports a bad answer.

Watch a few numbers on a dashboard: error rate, latency, cost per request, and quality signals such as thumbs up/down or eval scores on a sample of live traffic. Set alerts so you hear about problems before your users complain.

Also watch for **drift**: the world changes. Users start asking new kinds of questions, or a provider updates a model, and quality quietly drops. Comparing this week's inputs and scores with last week's catches drift early. A common score is the Population Stability Index (PSI), where values above about 0.2 suggest real change.
The code wraps a fake model in a tracing decorator, simulates two weeks of traffic, and raises a drift alert when users start writing much longer prompts.
keyIdeas: A trace records everything about one request: inputs, outputs, time, cost.
Dashboards track error rate, latency, cost and quality.
Drift means inputs or quality change over time; compare periods.
Feed bad live examples back into your eval set.

options: A record of everything that happened during one request
A drawing of the model's architecture
quiz.explain: Traces capture inputs, steps, outputs, latency and cost so you can debug.

quiz.q: Your app's answers slowly get worse because users ask about new topics. This is called:
quiz.explain: Drift is when real-world data shifts away from what the system was built and tested on.

code.title: trace_and_drift.py
code.source:
# Trace every model call, then check whether inputs are drifting.
import time, random
import numpy as np

traces = []

def traced(fn):
    def wrapper(prompt):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        out = fn(prompt)
        traces.append({"prompt_words": len(prompt.split()), "answer_words": len(out.split()),
                       "ms": (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000, "error": out == ""})
        return out
    return wrapper

@traced
def fake_llm(prompt):
    return "" if random.random() < 0.05 else "ok " * random.randint(5, 40)

random.seed(0)
for _ in range(200):
    fake_llm("word " * random.randint(5, 30))      # last week's traffic
for _ in range(200):
    fake_llm("word " * random.randint(20, 60))     # this week: users write longer prompts

lengths = np.array([t["prompt_words"] for t in traces])
old, new = lengths[:200], lengths[200:]
print(f"Error rate          : {np.mean([t['error'] for t in traces]):.1%}")
print(f"Prompt length before: mean {old.mean():.1f} words")
print(f"Prompt length now   : mean {new.mean():.1f} words")

# Population Stability Index: > 0.2 usually means "real drift, take a look"
bins = np.histogram_bin_edges(lengths, bins=8)
p = np.histogram(old, bins)[0] / len(old) + 1e-4
q = np.histogram(new, bins)[0] / len(new) + 1e-4
psi = np.sum((q - p) * np.log(q / p))
print(f"PSI = {psi:.2f} -> {'DRIFT ALERT' if psi > 0.2 else 'stable'}")

lessons.title: LLMOps end to end
lessons.summary: Choose a model, iterate, test, deploy and monitor.

resources.title: Chip Huyen: Building LLM applications for production

body: **LLMOps** is the practice of taking an LLM app from idea to production and keeping it healthy. It joins everything from this course into one repeating loop.

The loop goes: **choose a model** (start with a strong one to prove the idea, then try cheaper ones), **iterate** on prompts, retrieval and tools, **test** every change against your eval set, **deploy**, and **monitor** live traffic. Problems found in monitoring become new test cases, and the loop starts again.

Treat prompts like code. Keep them in version control, give each version a name, and never ship a change just because it looked good on one example. A change only goes live if it scores at least as well as what is in production, like a new recipe that must pass a taste test before it goes on the menu.
Roll changes out carefully: try new versions on a small share of traffic first, compare the numbers, and keep the old version ready so you can roll back quickly if something goes wrong.
The code runs a mini release pipeline: two candidate prompt versions are evaluated against production. One is deployed and the other, which broke something, is rejected automatically.
keyIdeas: LLMOps loop: choose, iterate, test, deploy, monitor, repeat.
Version your prompts and configs like code.
Ship only changes that beat production on your evals.
Roll out gradually and keep a fast rollback ready.

quiz.q: A new prompt looks great on a few examples but scores lower on the eval set. What should you do?
options: Do not deploy; investigate the failing cases
quiz.explain: The eval set is the safety gate; a lower score means the change makes things worse overall.

quiz.q: Where do new test cases often come from in a mature LLMOps loop?
options: Failures found while monitoring live traffic
quiz.explain: Real-world failures make the test set more realistic over time.
